heard: That famous beam of light-cradling Earth was just camera glare. In 1990, NASA's Voyager 1 looked back across roughly 4 billion miles to photograph home. Astronomer Carl Sagan fought for years to take it, despite officials fearing the sun would destroy the optics. NASA Administrator Richard truly approved the 60-frame sequence, and the probe fired its cameras one final time before shutting them down forever. Most people see a poetic sunbeam miraculously illuminating our lonely blue world. In reality, that dramatic ray was merely sunlight bouncing off the spacecraft's own camera sunshade. Even more humbling, our entire planet does not even fill a dot, taking up only 0.12 of a single pixel. All of human history was captured as a fraction of a pixel inside an accidental reflection.
